title: Adjoint-gradient check (adjoint vs finite difference): is the gradient right?
summary: Before training with a hand-derived or adjoint gradient, check it against finite differences. Two panels: a parity plot of the two gradients, and the absolute error per parameter on a log axis with the finite-difference noise floor.

media.alt: Two panels: left, a parity scatter of adjoint gradient against finite-difference gradient for 40 parameters lying on the y = x line from -20 to 6; right, a log plot of absolute error per parameter index, mostly between 2e-9 and 1e-7 with one point at about 1e-6, and a dashed rose line at 1e-9 labelled FD floor.
media.caption: Reference render of class F6.8 (design-system gallery). The data are synthetic and exist only to demonstrate the form.

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: Is the gradient right?
read_the_figure.axes: Left: adjoint gradient (x) against finite-difference gradient (y), linear, with the line y = x. Right: parameter index 0 to 39 (x) against absolute error |adjoint - FD| (y, logarithmic from 1e-11 to 1e-3).
look_at: Do the points lie on y = x over the whole range of gradient values?
How large is the absolute error, and how does it compare with the floor line?
Is there any parameter whose error stands out?
Is the floor line explained (which difference scheme and which h)?
as_drawn: Forty parameters with gradients from about -20 to +6; all points lie on the line y = x at the scale of the left panel.
The error panel shows stems from about 2e-9 up to 1e-7 for most parameters, with a median near 9e-9, and one outlier near 1.2e-6 at index 38.
The dashed floor is at about 1e-9, labelled as the finite-difference floor for a central difference with h = 1e-5. No error stem falls below it; most lie one to two decades above.

The text box in the middle says the error sits at the FD floor and the adjoint gradient is correct; this overstates what the stems show (they are above the line), and the box covers part of the stems.
read_the_figure.proves: Agreement far below the size of the gradient, at the level expected from the finite-difference scheme itself, is strong evidence that the adjoint (or analytic) gradient is implemented correctly. It does not prove the loss it differentiates is the right loss.
if_wrong: Parity points off the diagonal: the gradient is wrong, often by a missing term or a sign.
Errors that do not shrink when h is varied: not a finite-difference artefact; the adjoint is wrong.
Errors for a few parameters much larger than the rest: check those parameters' code paths.
must_check: log error: the errors span many decades and what matters is their order of magnitude, which a linear axis cannot show.
FD floor line: it tells the reader how small an error can be expected from finite differences alone, and so what counts as agreement.

terms.meaning: The gradient of a loss with respect to many parameters, computed with one backward solve rather than one solve per parameter.
An approximation of a derivative by differences of function values.
The symmetric difference above; its truncation error is of order h squared.
The smallest error a finite-difference gradient can reach: truncation falls with h, round-off grows like 1/h.
A scatter of one estimate against another; points on y = x mean agreement.

remember: Central difference error is about (h^2 / 6) |f'''| + epsilon |f| / h.
Best h is about (3 epsilon |f| / |f'''|)^(1/3), near 1e-5 for unit scales.
Always judge agreement on a log scale and relative to the size of the gradient.
A parity plot hides errors smaller than the marker.

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Left: each point is one parameter; its horizontal position is the adjoint gradient and its vertical position the finite-difference gradient; the dashed line is perfect agreement. Right: each vertical stem is one parameter's absolute error on a log axis; the dashed rose line is the expected finite-difference floor. The pair shows the same agreement at two scales.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Plain language: a gradient computed by a clever method is easy to get slightly wrong, and a slightly wrong gradient makes training fail without any error message. A finite difference is slow but simple, so it is the reference. Putting the two on a parity plot shows large errors at once; the log error panel shows small ones and tells you whether they are at the level that finite differences themselves can reach.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: On the left panel, errors of 1e-8 are invisible: all gradients look perfect. On the right, the floor depends on h and the size of the function: using the wrong h makes a correct gradient look wrong or a wrong one look right. In this render the stems lie above the floor line, so the sentence in the text box is stronger than the data. Absolute errors say little for a parameter whose gradient is near zero; relative errors do.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A table of relative errors with the number of correct digits per parameter, or a plot of the error against the step h for one parameter (a V-shaped curve whose minimum is the floor), shows the same check more directly. A random-direction test, comparing the directional derivative along a random vector, checks all parameters at once at little cost.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Plot relative error, draw the error against h for three parameters in a third panel to show the V shape, and mark the acceptance threshold you use, say 1e-6.

steps.title: Central difference and its error
steps.note: Truncation error of order h squared.

steps.title: Round-off and the floor
steps.note: With unit scales h* is about 8.7e-6. At h = 1e-5 and |J| near 50 the round-off term is 1.1e-9, the floor drawn in the render.

steps.title: A relative check
steps.note: A floor g_ref avoids dividing by a gradient that is almost zero; choose it from the typical size of the gradient.

worked.title: Reading the gradient check in the reference render
worked.problem: (1) What range of gradients is covered and do all points lie on the diagonal? (2) How does the typical error compare with the floor line, and which parameter is the outlier? (3) What size of function value would give a round-off floor of 1e-9 at h = 1e-5?

solution.text: (1) The gradients run from about -20 to +6 and every point sits on y = x at the scale of the panel.

(2) The stems start at 2e-9, the median is near 9e-9 and the largest is about 1.2e-6 at parameter 38. The floor is 1e-9, so the typical error is about ten times the floor line and the outlier is a thousand times the floor line and worth a second look.

worked.answer: Gradients from -20 to 6 on the diagonal; typical errors of about 9e-9, ten times the floor line, and one outlier at 1.2e-6 (parameter 38); a floor of 1e-9 corresponds to a function value of about 45.

analyze.q: The text box in the render says the error sits at the floor. Do you agree with the picture?
analyze.hint: Compare the stems with the dashed line.

analyze.q: Why do you need the right panel if the left panel shows perfect agreement?
analyze.hint: Marker size and the scale of the gradients.

analyze.q: How would you decide whether the outlier at parameter 38 is a bug?
analyze.hint: Repeat with several h and use a relative error.

evaluate.q: A gradient check passes on one random input and one random parameter vector. Is the adjoint validated?
evaluate.hint: Other inputs, edge cases, other regimes.

create: Redraw the right panel as relative error and add the V-shaped error against h for three chosen parameters.
Implement a random-direction check and show its error beside the per-parameter check.

checks.q: Why check an adjoint gradient against finite differences?
checks.hint: Which is simpler to get right?
checks.answer: A finite difference needs only function values and is hard to get wrong, so it is a reference for the more complex adjoint code.

checks.q: A central difference with h = 1e-4 and a function value of order 1 has what truncation error if f''' is about 1?
checks.answer: 1e-8 / 6 = 1.7e-9; the round-off term at this h is about 2e-12.

checks.q: All points on the left panel lie on y = x, but one error stem is at 1e-6 while the others are near 1e-8. What do you do?
checks.answer: Check that parameter's relative error and repeat with other h; if it persists it points to a bug in that parameter's code path, if it varies with h it is a finite-difference artefact.
